title: ‘I Welcome Their Hatred’
gist: On the 90th anniversary of FDR's 1936 'I welcome their hatred' Madison Square Garden speech, Tinline traces how British and U.S. center-left figures are reviving it as a model for beating right-wing populism with a polarizing message in a non-polarizing tone. The open question is which enemy to target: bond markets (tried by new UK PM Andy Burnham), gambling firms, privatized utilities, tax-exile tycoons, or big tech and Elon Musk.

insights.claim: In his Oct. 31, 1936 Madison Square Garden speech, Roosevelt charged that 'government by organized money' was as dangerous as 'government by organized mob,' and three days later won almost 61% of the vote.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Historical precedent that confronting concentrated corporate power can be electorally decisive.
insights.quote: “Government by organized money,” he charged, was “just as dangerous as government by organized mob.”
insights.locator: Roosevelt realized that by facing down

insights.claim: Roosevelt turned combative after the Supreme Court blocked New Deal programs like the National Recovery Administration and newspapers and tycoons grew hostile.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Institutional obstruction can radicalize centrist governments toward anti-business rhetoric.

insights.claim: Tinline's thesis is that FDR's lines landed because they came from a cool-tempered centrist driven to declare vested interests had gone too far, not from an angry leftist.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Anti-corporate populism from mainstream leaders is more potent, and more policy-relevant, than from the fringe.
insights.quote: Those lines landed precisely because they were not delivered by an angry leftist, but a cool-tempered centrist, driven finally to declare that the vested interests had gone too far.
insights.locator: The real lesson of the speech

themes.theme: UK center-left search for a populist response

insights.claim: In the 2024 UK election, support for far-right Reform UK hit 14% and has continued to rise, while Starmer's managerial approach left liberal-left critics fearful.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Rising Reform UK support is a key UK political risk variable.

insights.claim: Starmer has been replaced as prime minister by former Greater Manchester mayor Andy Burnham, a politician much more ready to talk about power.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: UK leadership has shifted to a more combative Labour figure, raising odds of interventionist economic rhetoric.
insights.locator: Starmer didn’t have it in him

insights.claim: Pollster Peter Kellner urged Starmer to 'declare war' on Brexit's champions, saying the risk was the point.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: Shows pressure within UK commentariat for confrontational Labour strategy.
insights.quote: “Would he be taking a risk?” Kellner added. “Absolutely — and that’s the point.”
insights.locator: Writing in Prospect magazine, Ben Ansell

insights.claim: Guardian historian Andy Beckett says the consensual 1990s social-democratic tone has been 'tested to destruction' and that amid economic insecurity and extreme inequality social democracy must be much more aggressive rhetorically.
insights.speaker: Andy Beckett
insights.so_what: Signals a turn toward redistributive, anti-incumbent-interest policy rhetoric on the center-left.

insights.claim: Robert Ford argues the left and radical right are coalescing around in-group/out-group politics at a mass level regardless of what politicians do, and FDR offered 'a polarizing message in a non-polarizing tone' that Burnham is well-placed to copy.
insights.speaker: Robert Ford
insights.so_what: Structural polarization means corporate villains are likely targets for mainstream parties.

insights.claim: Advocates point to punchier approaches by Spain's and Australia's prime ministers and to Manuela Schwesig holding back the AfD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Combative center-left tactics are being tested across several democracies.
insights.locator: Starmer didn’t have it in him

themes.theme: Choosing the enemy: markets, utilities, big tech

insights.claim: Oxford's Ben Ansell says Burnham tried targeting the bond markets, which 'didn't work quite so brilliantly.'
insights.speaker: Ben Ansell
insights.so_what: Gilt-market pushback has already constrained a UK government's populist rhetoric, a key gilt risk signal.

insights.claim: Ansell suggests Labour could more fruitfully target exploitative gambling companies, tax-exiled right-wing tycoons, or the heads of the UK's notoriously inefficient privatized utilities.
insights.speaker: Ben Ansell
insights.so_what: UK gambling and privatized utility sectors face elevated political and regulatory risk.

insights.claim: Robert Ford argues Labour should target big tech, specifically Elon Musk, who is very unpopular in the UK after inflammatory interventions and the scandal over his AI Grok producing child sexual abuse images.
insights.speaker: Robert Ford
insights.so_what: Musk-linked businesses and big tech face heightened UK regulatory and political hostility.
insights.quote: “a golden opportunity for any center-left populist looking to do a bit of an FDR.”

insights.claim: In 2025, Elon Musk appeared by video at an extreme-right rally in London and told the crowd 'you either fight back or you die.'
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Musk's political profile is a reputational risk factor for his companies in Europe.

themes.theme: U.S. progressive use of FDR rhetoric

insights.claim: In the U.S., FDR's speech has been embraced mainly by those to Obama's left, including Elizabeth Warren, Bernie Sanders and Jamie Raskin, who used it to endorse New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Anti-corporate framing is concentrated on the progressive wing of U.S. politics.
insights.locator: Elizabeth Warren has embraced the speech

insights.claim: Rep. Greg Casar used the speech to launch the Congressional Progressive Caucus' 10-plank midterm agenda focused on stopping corporate 'price gouging' and curbing Super PAC spending.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Price-gouging legislation is a potential policy risk for consumer-facing corporates if Democrats gain.
insights.locator: In April, Democratic Rep. Greg Casar

insights.claim: Tinline argues Casar's approach of uniting left and moderate Democrats around economic policies redirecting populist anger toward cost-of-living culprits is effective, but moderates may need to go beyond attacks on 'billionaires' and 'the Epstein class.'
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Cost-of-living populism is likely central to Democratic messaging and potential corporate-targeted policy.
insights.locator: Casar’s approach seems much more effective
